items.prompt: What are the two main types of venomous snakes, named after the way their fangs are arranged?

options.label: Constrictors and swimmers
options.feedback: Constrictors squeeze prey and have no venom fangs at all. The two groups with venom fangs are the viperids and elapids.

options.label: Burrowers and climbers
options.feedback: Burrowing and climbing describe where a snake lives, not the arrangement of its venom fangs. Viperids and elapids are the two named fang groups.

options.label: Viperids and elapids
options.feedback: Correct. Viperids, like rattlesnakes, have long folding front fangs; elapids, like cobras, have short fixed front fangs.

options.label: Rear-fanged and legless
options.feedback: Rear-fanged is a category for some snakes, but legless describes all snakes. The two main groups are viperids and elapids.

items.ok_line: Viperids fold long fangs, elapids keep short fixed ones.
items.ko_line: Check the fang types, not where snakes live.
items.exp_text: Venomous snakes are divided by how their fangs sit in the mouth. Viperids have long, hollow fangs that fold back when not in use; elapids have short, fixed fangs at the front. The fang arrangement is the key difference, not behavior or habitat.

items.prompt: What is the soft, stretchy material that a snake's fangs are made of, similar to what human teeth have?

options.label: Cartilage
options.feedback: Cartilage is found in joints and ears, not in teeth. Fangs are made of dentin, like human teeth.

options.label: Dentin
options.feedback: Correct. Fang walls are composed of dentin, the same hard but slightly flexible material that makes up most of a human tooth.

options.label: Keratin
options.feedback: Keratin makes hair and scales, not teeth. Fangs use dentin, a tooth material.

options.label: Bone
options.feedback: Bone is harder and less flexible than tooth material. Fangs are dentin, not bone.

items.ok_line: Dentin gives fangs strength without brittleness.
items.ko_line: Remember fangs are teeth, so they share tooth chemistry.
items.exp_text: Snake fangs are hollow teeth. Their walls are made of dentin, the same material that forms the bulk of human teeth. Dentin is hard enough to pierce skin but slightly flexible, so fangs bend a little without snapping during a strike.

items.prompt: In which part of a snake's head are its venom glands located?

options.label: Behind the eyes
options.feedback: Correct. Venom glands sit on each side of the head, just behind the eyes, which is why many venomous snakes have a wider, triangular head.

options.label: In the lower jaw
options.feedback: The lower jaw holds teeth but no venom glands. Glands are behind the eyes, not in the jaw.

options.label: In the roof of the mouth
options.feedback: The roof of the mouth has some sensory cells, but venom is produced in glands behind the eyes.

options.label: At the tip of the tongue
options.feedback: The tongue is for sensing smell, not venom. Glands are behind the eyes.

items.ok_line: Look behind the eyes for venom production.
items.ko_line: The glands are not in the mouth or tongue.
items.exp_text: Each venomous snake has a pair of glands positioned behind the eyes, one on each side of the skull. This placement gives many venomous snakes their characteristic broad, triangular head shape, distinguishing them from non-venomous species with slimmer heads.

items.prompt: What is the name of the special opening at the tip of a viper's hollow fang through which venom is injected?

options.label: Pore
options.feedback: A pore is a general hole, but the fang's exit has a specific name: the venom canal's opening is called the orifice.

options.label: Nostril
options.feedback: Nostrils are for breathing, not venom. The fang's exit is the orifice.

options.label: Groove
options.feedback: A groove is an open channel on the surface; vipers have a closed tube with an exit called the orifice.

options.label: Orifice
options.feedback: Correct. The venom runs down the hollow core of the fang and exits through a small opening near the tip called the orifice.

items.ok_line: Venom leaves through the orifice at the fang tip.
items.ko_line: It is a sealed tube, not an open groove or pore.
items.exp_text: A viper's fang is like a hypodermic needle: a hard outer shell with a hollow channel inside. At the tip, this channel opens to the outside through a small hole called the orifice. When the snake bites, muscles squeeze the gland, forcing venom down the fang and out this orifice into the prey.

items.prompt: What is the fluid called that a snake's fangs inject into its prey to kill or weaken it?

options.label: Saliva
options.feedback: Saliva is a digestive fluid in the mouth, but the injected toxin has a distinct name: venom.

options.label: Venom
options.feedback: Correct. Venom is a specialized toxic secretion produced in modified salivary glands and delivered through fangs.

options.label: Bile
options.feedback: Bile is produced in the liver for digestion, not in the fangs. The injected substance is venom.

options.label: Mucus
options.feedback: Mucus is a slippery protective coating, not a toxin. Venom is what the fangs inject.

items.ok_line: Venom is the toxic fluid from the glands.
items.ko_line: Think of the specialized secretion, not ordinary body fluids.
items.exp_text: Venom is a complex mixture of proteins and enzymes produced in modified salivary glands. It is injected through fangs to disable prey. Unlike saliva, which only starts digestion in the mouth, venom has specialized toxins that act on the nervous system, blood, or muscles.

items.prompt: What is the name of the long, hollow tube that runs from the venom gland to the base of the fang?

options.label: Artery
options.feedback: An artery carries blood, not venom. The venom path is called the venom duct.

options.label: Trachea
options.feedback: The trachea is the windpipe for breathing, not for venom. The duct connects the gland to the fang.

options.label: Venom duct
options.feedback: Correct. The venom duct is a thin canal that carries venom from the gland down to the hollow fang's base.

options.label: Esophagus
options.feedback: The esophagus carries food to the stomach, not venom. The venom duct is the correct structure.

items.ok_line: The venom duct links gland to fang.
items.ko_line: It is a gland duct, not a circulatory or digestive tube.
items.exp_text: Venom flows from the gland through a slender tube called the venom duct, which leads directly to the hollow base of the fang. Muscles around the gland contract to squeeze venom out, so the duct acts as a one-way pipe ensuring the venom reaches the fang rather than leaking into the mouth.

items.prompt: What is the term for the small, non-venomous teeth that a snake uses to grip prey before or after the fangs strike?

options.label: Palatine teeth
options.feedback: Correct. Palatine teeth are small curved teeth on the roof of the mouth that help hold and pull prey in.

options.label: Molars
options.feedback: Molars are flat grinding teeth found in mammals, not in snakes. Snake teeth are all pointed for gripping.

options.label: Incisors
options.feedback: Incisors are front cutting teeth in mammals. Snakes have palatine teeth for gripping, not cutting.

options.label: Canines
options.feedback: Canines are long pointed teeth for tearing, but snakes use palatine teeth in the roof of the mouth.

items.ok_line: Palatine teeth hold prey in place.
items.ko_line: Snakes lack molars, incisors, or canines.
items.exp_text: Snakes have several small, backward-curved teeth on the roof of the mouth, called palatine teeth. These teeth are not venomous; they act like tiny hooks. When the snake swallows, these teeth catch on the prey's skin and pull it further into the throat, preventing the prey from slipping back out.

items.prompt: Which part of a snake's body has a specialized heat-sensing pit that detects warm-blooded prey?

options.label: The tail
options.feedback: The tail may have a rattle in some species, but heat pits are on the face, not the tail.

options.label: The belly scales
options.feedback: Belly scales help movement, not heat sensing. Pits are facial features.

options.label: The tongue
options.feedback: The tongue senses chemicals in the air, not heat. Heat pits are located on the head.

options.label: The face, between the nostril and eye
options.feedback: Correct. Pit vipers have a heat-sensing pit on each side of the head, between the nostril and the eye, which detects infrared radiation.

items.ok_line: Pits sit on the face between nostril and eye.
items.ko_line: Heat detection is a head feature, not a tail or skin one.
items.exp_text: Pit vipers, like rattlesnakes and copperheads, have a pair of deep pits on their faces—one on each side, between the nostril and the eye. These pits contain a membrane rich in nerve endings that can detect the infrared heat radiating from warm-blooded animals, allowing the snake to hunt in total darkness.

items.prompt: What is the main chemical component of a snake's venom that attacks the nervous system of the prey?

options.label: Enzymes
options.feedback: Enzymes break down tissues and start digestion, but the nerve-attacking component is specifically a neurotoxin.

options.label: Neurotoxins
options.feedback: Correct. Neurotoxins interfere with nerve signals, causing paralysis and stopping breathing.

options.label: Anticoagulants
options.feedback: Anticoagulants prevent blood clotting, but they don't attack nerves. Neurotoxins do that.

options.label: Hemotoxins
options.feedback: Hemotoxins damage blood cells and vessels, not the nervous system. Neurotoxins target nerves.

items.ok_line: Neurotoxins paralyze by blocking nerve signals.
items.ko_line: Only neurotoxins directly affect the nervous system.
items.exp_text: Venom is a cocktail of different molecules. Neurotoxins are the ones that bind to nerve cells and prevent them from sending messages to muscles. This can cause rapid paralysis, so the prey cannot escape or breathe. Other venom components may digest tissues or disrupt blood, but neurotoxins specifically target the nervous system.

items.prompt: What is the term for a snake's fangs that are located at the back of its mouth, rather than the front?

options.label: Front-fanged
options.feedback: Front-fanged describes fangs at the front, like in vipers and cobras. Back fangs are called rear-fanged.

options.label: Fixed-fanged
options.feedback: Fixed-fanged refers to fangs that cannot fold, not their position. Rear-fanged is about location.

options.label: Rear-fanged
options.feedback: Correct. Rear-fanged snakes have venom-conducting fangs at the back of their upper jaw, used to chew venom into prey.

options.label: Hollow-fanged
options.feedback: Hollow-fanged describes the internal structure, not the position. The correct positional term is rear-fanged.

items.ok_line: Rear-fanged snakes chew venom into prey.
items.ko_line: Position refers to front or rear, not folding or hollowness.
items.exp_text: Some venomous snakes, like the boomslang, have their fangs set far back on the upper jaw. These are called rear-fanged snakes. Because the fangs are not at the front, they cannot strike as easily; instead, they must grab prey and chew, working the back fangs into the wound to deliver venom.
